extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical poetics, literary critics, dramatists studying Aristotle
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for composing and judging tragedy and poetic imitation according to Aristotle's Poetics: what tragedy is, its essential parts, and the qualities (unity, magnitude, diction, melody, spectacle, effects) that make it effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (mimesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitatio — the fundamental poetic faculty: imitation by means of rhythm, language, and melody; a natural human instinct present from childhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle describes imitation as a pleasure-giving, innate activity by which humans learn ("imitatio res est quae crescit cum hominibus...") and as the basis of all poetic forms; imitation may take different metres and rhythms but remains the central principle of poetic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy defined (essence of the genre)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Tragoedia imitatio operis voluntarii studiosi, et perfecti, habens magnitudinem in sermone utili ... faciens in partibus non per pollicitationes et aequat passiones per misericordiam et metum et purgat illos qui patiuntur" — tragedy imitates a serious, complete action of some magnitude in embellished language and rhythm/melody, and through pity and fear effects a purgation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A full definition encompassing: the object (a voluntary action), the seriousness (studious/seria), completeness (perfecti), magnitude (magnitudinem), medium (sermo with rhythm and melody), and function (to arouse pity/fear and to purge/catharsis). Use this as the primary checklist for whether a work qualifies as tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness of subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy treats serious (seria) subjects — not trivial or purely comic material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The material should be grave and important in tone and consequence (contrasting with comedy, which treats the 'pravior' or laughable). Seriousness is part of what makes an imitation tragic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness / Unity (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy (or any whole) must have an initium, medium, et finem — a beginning, middle, and end — such that the beginning is not necessarily with another, the middle is with both, and the end is such that nothing follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot must be a complete whole: the arrangement of incidents should be such that the sequence produces a coherent causal and temporal unity. The critic should check for a clear outset, a connected middle, and a conclusive end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude (length/scale appropriate to effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy must have a certain magnitude (longitudo/magnitudo) — not too small — such that the whole is apprehensible and memorable; length should suit the nature of the action and be sufficient for its completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnitude is judged by whether the work can be apprehended as a whole (e.g., in a single performance or within a reasonable time), whether its length preserves memory and effect, and whether the scale allows proper unfolding of beginning, middle, and end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis: arousal and purgation of pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy should arouse pity (misericordiam) and fear (metum) and effect a purgation (purgat) of these emotions in the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should consider whether the incidents and presentation evoke genuine pity and fear and whether the overall effect resolves or purges those emotions rather than merely sensationalizing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot / Constitution of action (fabulae / constitutio rerum)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot (fabula, constitutione rerum) is the chief element of tragedy — imitation of actions and life, not of persons; it is the arrangement of events (with initium, medium, finem) and is superior in importance to other parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should prioritize the integrity and causal organization of events, the presence of recognitions and reversals (circumvolutio et recognitio are noted as parts of fabula), and whether the plot produces the requisite emotional and intellectual effects. Plot is the decisive factor in tragic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot sub-elements: complication and recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Components of the fabula include circumvolutio (complication/turning) and recognitio (recognition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good tragedy typically employs structured complication and instances of recognition/reversal to produce surprise, emotional shifts, and the movement toward catharsis; their presence and handling are evaluative points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters / Consuetudines
rubrics_metrics.description: Consuetudines (habits/character dispositions) are the parts whereby poets show how persons will act — the moral/psychological traits that motivate actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character is important but subordinate to plot: evaluate whether characters' habits and dispositions are credible, consistent, and suitably revealed through action to support the plot and elicit audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought / Creditum (dianoia; 'what is said')
rubrics_metrics.description: Creditum (thought) is the intellectual content or reasoning expressed — the part that shows the speaker's intention and argumentative quality ('vis narrandi' and what the speakers intend or prove).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the quality of ideas, arguments, themes, and the appropriateness of the characters' reasoning to their situation; distinguish modes of delivery (earlier poets used political style, later rhetoric) and judge fit for genre and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction / Language (dictio / lexis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dictio signifies the composition of metres and the choice of language and phrasing (poetic diction, metre, rhetorical devices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the suitability and skill of language: metre selection, rhetorical quality, appropriateness of elevated or plain speech to the characters and situations, and how diction supports rhythm, melody, and the dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody / Song (melodia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Melodia (musical element) is an essential component of tragedy — parts of song and musical accompaniment embedded in the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the integration of song and musical rhythms with spoken parts; melody contributes to the emotional and formal unity of the piece and should harmonize with metre and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle / Visual element (aspectus / ops soni/visus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspectus (spectacle, the visual representation) and the external effect of stagecraft are influential but are not the primary art of the poet; spectacle is more a matter of performance (hypocrites/actors, stagecraft) than poetic composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge spectacle's power to move the audience, but place lower weight on it when evaluating poetic/artistic merit; prefer plot and language as the measure of poetic quality rather than scenic display alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of metre and rhythm to genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Different metres and rhythms suit different genres (e.g., iambus associated with certain types, tetrameters used for satyric/choric elements); poets may combine metres but must match metre to the nature of the imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether metre and rhythm fit the nature of the action and speech (e.g., lyric passages, choruses, satyric origins), and whether changes of metre support or undermine the work's unity and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: imitation of the 'pravior' and its aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Comoedia is imitation of the inferior (pravioris), not in every vice but in the laughable; it treats the ridiculous (ridicula) — ugliness that is not painful or harmful — and aims to provoke laughter rather than pity/fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating comedy, check that the objects of ridicule are appropriate (ridiculous without causing real harm), that the tone suits the comedic aim, and that the imitation exploits faults that are laughable rather than dangerous or purely malicious.
